title: Why Prevention Comes First
brief: Open by establishing the unit's core argument: that effective behaviour management is primarily about preventing problems before they arise, not reacting to them after the fact. Draw on the source's framing of classroom management as something built over time through routines, environment, and engagement — for example, the observation that the teacher in the video 'has developed routines that include students in classroom management processes' over a ten-month school year. Explain that a well-organised, stimulating, and comfortable environment reduces the conditions in which off-task behaviour occurs, citing the source's statement that 'students need an environment that is organized, stimulating, and comfortable in order to learn effectively.' Introduce the idea that prevention is positive and practical, not punitive, and that this approach works across age groups, with differences noted where relevant throughout the unit.

title: Building Routines That Students Own
brief: Focus on classroom routines as the primary prevention tool, drawing directly on the source's examples of routines used with very young learners that can be adapted for other ages. Cover the source's point that 'establishing routines can help younger students become more well-behaved and autonomous learners,' and give concrete examples from the source: the 'hello' song at the start of class, the student helper who calls names one by one for learning stations, and the clean-up routine reinforced with positive phrases. Explain how routines give students a sense of ownership and responsibility — the source notes students are 'allowed to choose so that they can enjoy their learning experience and take responsibility for their own learning.' Address adaptation for older learners by drawing on the source's prompt about how routines developed for very young learners could be modified for older students, keeping the section practical and age-aware without being prescriptive.

title: Clear and Fair Expectations
brief: Cover the importance of making behavioural expectations explicit, visible, and co-constructed with students. Draw on the source's guidance that teachers should 'let students help to define appropriate behavior for each station' and 'post activity guidelines and behavior rules (text or signs with pictures) at each learning station.' Explain that expectations should be taught, not just stated — the source recommends that teachers 'help students learn how to behave appropriately by role-playing and practicing with them.' Discuss how clarity of expectation reduces ambiguity and therefore reduces disruption, linking this to the source's advice that students need 'clear guidelines' covering when to move, how long to stay, how to transition, how to clean up, and how to interact respectfully with peers. Note that posting rules with pictures supports learners at different language or literacy levels, making this approach inclusive across age groups.

title: Engagement as a Management Strategy
brief: Argue that keeping students actively engaged is itself a behaviour management technique, drawing on the source's description of lessons that use 'movement, repetition, and several types of activities to engage the young students.' Use the source's examples of engagement tools — puppets, songs, games, learning stations with student choice, and content-based instruction — to show how varied, stimulating activity reduces the likelihood of off-task behaviour. Reference the source's observation that the teacher 'uses a variety of techniques to encourage good behavior and create a positive learning environment for these lively students.' Include the source's point about separating high-activity stations from quieter ones as a practical way to manage energy levels in the room. Briefly note that while the source's examples focus on younger learners, the principle of varied, purposeful activity applies across age groups, with the specific tools adapted accordingly.

title: Positive and Calm Responses to Disruption
brief: Address what teachers should do when disruption does occur, keeping the tone positive and practical in line with the unit's scope. Draw on the source's concrete examples of teacher language used to redirect attention calmly: phrases such as 'Put your listening ears on,' 'Turn your lips off,' and 'Let me see your body crisscross applesauce.' Contrast these with punitive approaches by emphasising the source's framing of 'positive reward systems for on-task, appropriate behavior' as the recommended tool. Use the source's examples of positive reinforcement language — 'Good job cleaning up,' 'I like how X is sitting,' 'Thank you for cleaning up' — to show how naming and praising appropriate behaviour publicly redirects the group without singling out individuals negatively. Note that the source also describes the teacher managing 'situations involving distractions and off-task students' through encouragement and feedback techniques rather than punishment, reinforcing the unit's positive and practical stance.

title: Managing Transitions Between Activities
brief: Dedicate this section to transitions as a specific and often underestimated behaviour management challenge. Draw on the source's explicit acknowledgement that 'managing transitions between activities can be difficult, especially when working with very young learners,' and extend this to other age groups. Use the source's examples of transition techniques: the teacher signals attention with specific phrases and songs, calls students to stations one by one rather than all at once to avoid chaos, and uses a student helper to manage the flow. Cover the source's practical advice that students need guidelines for 'how to make smooth transitions in/out stations' and 'how to clean up at the end of station time.' Encourage trainees to think about which signals and routines they could adapt for their own context, drawing on the source's reflective prompt about adapting transition techniques 'for use with your students,' and note that the principle of signalling clearly before a change applies across all age groups even if the specific signal differs.
